claims.text: A post-solidification heat treatment that converts a continuous brittle phase into discrete precipitates in a continuous ductile matrix will increase room-temperature tensile strength relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The same microstructural inversion will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The initial eutectic HEA consists of dual-phase lamellar colonies containing a continuous brittle ordered phase and a ductile phase.
The continuous brittle phase promotes microcrack initiation and premature tensile fracture.
High-temperature solutionizing, rapid quenching, and low-temperature annealing can induce the proposed phase-continuity inversion.
After treatment, the originally continuous brittle phase will re-precipitate as fine particles in a continuous ductile matrix.
The re-precipitated brittle particles will be coherent with the ductile matrix.
The intervention is applicable when the two constituent phases have a substantial contrast in intrinsic ductility and strength.
Avoiding full dissolution and excessive coarsening will cause the brittle phase to form as a dispersed nanoscale reinforcement rather than a continuous network.
The inverted structure comprises a continuous disordered FCC or BCC matrix reinforced by finely dispersed ordered precipitates.
Making the brittle phase discontinuous removes continuous preferential crack-propagation paths.
A continuous ductile matrix promotes uniform dislocation motion and delays crack initiation.
Fine coherent ordered precipitates strengthen the alloy by precipitation hardening without compromising ductility.
The modified alloy will have a higher ultimate tensile strength than the conventionally processed lamellar baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit more than a 20% increase in room-temperature elongation relative to the baseline.
Standard processing of eutectic HEAs typically produces a lamellar structure containing a continuous brittle ordered phase.
A continuous ordered phase can provide high strength while limiting deformation before fracture.
The benefit will not be realized when phase ductilities are too similar or when transformation kinetics do not permit controlled inversion.
The magnitude of the tensile-property improvement depends on composition and heat-treatment parameters.
